newsitem.title: USA: Lower U.S. rates continue to propel refinancings.
newsitem.headline: Lower U.S. rates continue to propel refinancings.

text.p: The mortgage industry has been experiencing a refinancing boomlet, as lower borrowing costs encouraged more U.S. homeowners to refinance their mortgages.
"Treasury yields are falling and therefore mortgage rates are falling," said Brian Carey, an economist with the Mortgage Bankers Association of America (MBA).
The MBA reported earlier that 31.4 percent of the mortgage banking activity was refinancing-related in the week ended July 25.
In the current rate environment, refinancings should not account for more than 40 percent of total application activity.
"For refinancings to hit 50 percent of total activity, rates would have to go down a lot further," said Carey.

The MBA reported total refinancings rose 9.8 percent in the week, while application activity rose 2.3 percent. The association's seasonally adjusted refinancing index rose 9.8 percent from the previous week to 595.9.
An index level over 500 signals a mini-refinancing boon, said Carey, who predicted the index may hit 700.
Carey said much of the refinancing activity occurred in 30-year fixed-rate mortgage loans and these should continue to decline this week.

The MBA economist said many consumers refinanced in 1992 and 1993 to lock in 30-year fixed rates at around 7.0 percent. He said any mortgage products with a rate of over 8.0 percent can be considered refinanceable.

Carey recalled that in February 1996, refinancings accounted for 50 percent of total mortgage applications, while the historical high came in January 1992, when refinancings enjoyed a 72-percent slice of total application business.

Carey said some mortgage loan originators would target their portfolios and telephone existing borrowers that they currently service. He was uncertain if lenders were stepping up advertising to lure borrowers away from competitors, but said current borrowers were sure to be solicited.

Refinancings for California mortgage loans were expected to see a pick-up in activity because of an improvement in that state's housing market. As home values rise, homeowners see the equity in their homes increase, allowing them to refinance.
"The California (housing) market lagged in the early- to mid-1990s and is picking up. Home prices depreciated in the 1990s so they (borrowers) were not able to refinance," the MBA economist said.

"We would expect that California would have a larger concentration of refinancings than some other states. Now that the housing market has come back, people who lost equity when their home values declined may refinance," said Carey.
